summary: InterGlobe Aviation runs IndiGo, India’s largest airline. It flies passengers between Indian cities and abroad on mostly leased Airbus planes, sells tickets and extras such as seats, bags and snacks, and carries cargo.
description: IndiGo sells seats on more than 2,000 flights a day to about 97 Indian and 45 foreign destinations, and in 2025–26 it carried about 123 million passengers. It flies 441 aircraft, mostly single-aisle Airbus jets; most are rented from aircraft-leasing companies rather than owned. Its annual report credits a young, fuel-efficient fleet and closely packed seating for keeping the fuel cost per seat low. A wholly owned company, Agile Airport Services, guides, loads and unloads its planes at airports, and another, based in the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) at GIFT City, buys planes and leases them to the airline.
money: Most income is passenger ticket revenue. Ancillary revenue adds money from cargo, extra baggage, booking fees, ticket changes and cancellations, seat choice and food sold on board. Fuel and the cost of owning or renting aircraft, including engine rentals and maintenance, are the largest costs, followed by staff and airport charges. Many of these are paid in US dollars, so a weaker rupee raises costs. A ticket sold for a future date is not revenue until the flight happens, and revenue is not profit.
customers: Mostly individual travellers, who pay for a ticket and sometimes extras; more choose its business-style IndiGoStretch seats or flexible fares. Companies ship goods in its planes’ holds and in a few freighter aircraft. Partner banks issue IndiGo co-branded credit cards that earn BluChip loyalty points. The airline holds over 60% of the Indian domestic market.
drivers: Average ticket prices and how full planes are, the price of jet fuel, the rupee against the dollar, and whether it has enough working aircraft and crew to fly its schedule.

groups.title: Flights within India
groups.examples: A morning flight from Delhi to Mumbai or Bengaluru to Kolkata.
groups.explanation: Short, frequent routes are the core of the business. The more seats sold on each flight and the higher the average fare, the more each flight earns.

groups.title: Flights abroad
groups.examples: Flights to the Gulf, South-East Asia and, with longer-range planes, Europe.
groups.explanation: International routes are a growing share of its seats. They earn some revenue in foreign currency, which offsets part of its dollar costs.

groups.title: Fare types and extras
groups.examples: Saver and Flexi fares, the roomier IndiGoStretch seats, seat choice, extra baggage and snacks on board.
groups.explanation: Passengers who want more pay more, either through a higher fare type or by adding services. These extras earn money without adding flights.

groups.title: Cargo
groups.examples: Parcels and goods carried under passenger cabins and in its freighter aircraft.
groups.explanation: Shippers pay to send goods. Cargo in passenger planes uses space on flights that are already flying.

groups.title: Loyalty programme
groups.examples: IndiGo BluChip points earned on flights and through co-branded credit cards.
groups.explanation: Members earn points they can spend on IndiGo flights, which encourages them to fly with IndiGo again.

basics.title: How do airlines measure their seats and sales?
basics.text: An available seat kilometre (ASK) is one seat flown one kilometre, the measure of capacity. Load factor is the share of seats filled. Yield is the average fare earned per kilometre a passenger flies.

basics.title: Why lease planes instead of buying them?
basics.text: Most IndiGo planes are on operating leases: it rents them from leasing companies instead of paying the full price up front. The rent is largely owed in US dollars over many years, so a weaker rupee makes these debts bigger.

basics.title: What are the crew duty rules?
basics.text: Flight Duty Time Limitation (FDTL) rules set how long pilots may fly and how much rest they must get. IndiGo says putting the revised rules into practice during a peak travel period contributed to delays and cancellations in December 2025.

steps.title: IndiGo plans routes and leases planes
steps.text: It decides which cities to link and how often, and takes delivery of aircraft, mostly on lease, years ahead.

steps.title: Passengers book and pay
steps.text: Customers buy tickets on its app, website or through agents, often weeks before flying. The money is received but held as owed to the customer until the flight.

steps.title: The flight operates
steps.text: Ground staff load bags and cargo, crew fly the plane and serve passengers, and fuel and airport charges are paid. Only now is the ticket counted as revenue.

steps.title: Extras and cargo add income
steps.text: Seat choices, bags, meals and changes bring extra fees; shippers pay for cargo carried on the same flights.

steps.title: Bills are paid
steps.text: IndiGo pays fuel suppliers, lessors, airports and staff. Revenue, profit after all these costs and cash in the bank are three different things.

specifics.title: A young, fuel-efficient fleet
specifics.text: Its planes averaged about 4.9 years old in March 2026, and about 79% were new-engine Airbus models that IndiGo says burn about 15% less fuel than the older type.

specifics.title: Size in a fast-growing market
specifics.text: It holds over 60% of the domestic market. Its annual report expects Indian air travel to keep growing with new airports and more international links.

specifics.title: Huge aircraft orders
specifics.text: It has orders for more than 900 aircraft, including longer-range Airbus A321XLR and wide-body A350 planes for flights to Europe and beyond.

specifics.title: Dollar debts on the books
specifics.text: Lease payments for its planes are owed in dollars over many years. When the rupee weakens, IndiGo records foreign exchange losses on these debts even before paying them.

watch: Are fares and load factors holding up?
Revenue depends on how full planes are and what each passenger pays.
Compare yield and load factor with the same quarter a year earlier in each quarterly press release.
Fuel is one of its largest costs and can jump with oil prices and wars.
Track fuel cost per available seat kilometre in each press release and the fuel-price comments in the annual report.
How much does the rupee hurt?
Many costs and lease debts are in dollars.
Compare profit with and without foreign exchange effects, which IndiGo shows separately in its press releases.
Is the international push paying off?
New long routes need new planes and time to fill seats.
Follow international capacity, load factor and destinations in the annual report’s operating table each year.
Cancellations, like those in December 2025, bring compensation costs, penalties and lost bookings.
Read on-time performance and cancellation rates in each press release, and any regulator orders mentioned in filings.
risks: The annual report calls aircraft fuel one of the largest costs; a sustained rise squeezes margins and forces fare increases.
Lease rentals, maintenance, airport charges and insurance are partly in foreign currency, so a falling rupee raises costs and creates exchange losses.
Conflicts can close airspace, forcing longer routes, more fuel use and cancellations on international flights.
Revised crew rest rules, introduced during a peak period, contributed to delays and cancellations; IndiGo set aside money for compensation, travel vouchers and a regulator penalty.
From 2026–27 it expects costs from an international carbon-offset scheme and rules requiring sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), which costs more than normal jet fuel.
Rivals adding planes and cutting fares can lower yields, market share and margins.
context: July to September 2026: higher fares, fewer passengers, costly fuel

On 29 October 2026 IndiGo reported results for July to September 2026. Compared with the same quarter a year earlier, it flew 1% less capacity and carried 27.5 million passengers, 4.7% fewer. Yield, the average fare per kilometre, rose 34.3% and revenue from operations 25.9%, but fuel cost per seat kilometre rose 68.9% and the rupee weakened, so it reported a net loss. This describes one quarter.
sources: Press release for the quarter ended 30 September 2026 (filed with NSE) · 29 October 2026

financialNotes.title: Separate the exchange-rate effect
financialNotes.text: IndiGo’s profit can swing on foreign exchange gains or losses on its dollar lease debts, so it also reports profit excluding those effects. Standalone (the airline) and consolidated (with its subsidiaries) results are separate. Verified full-year figures for this profile have not yet been added, so the financial table below is marked as awaiting verification.

stepsTitle: From a booked seat to a finished flight.

quick.title: What it does
quick.text: Flies passengers and cargo across India and abroad on a large fleet of mostly leased Airbus jets.

quick.title: Who pays
quick.text: Travellers pay for tickets and extras, and companies pay to send cargo.

quick.title: How it earns
quick.text: Mainly ticket sales, plus fees for bags, seats, changes, food on board and cargo.

quick.title: What it spends on
quick.text: Jet fuel, aircraft rent and maintenance, staff, and airport charges, many of them in US dollars.

helps.title: The biggest network in India
helps.text: Its annual report says it is positioned to benefit from rising air travel, new airports and more international links through its large domestic network.

helps.title: Low cost per seat
helps.text: A young fleet of fuel-efficient Airbus planes and high-density seating keep its cost per seat low, which the annual report names as a way it protects margins.

helps.title: Planes on order for years ahead
helps.text: An order book of more than 900 aircraft gives it clear capacity for future growth at home and abroad.

hurts.title: Costs it cannot control
hurts.text: Fuel prices and the rupee move with world events. The annual report lists both as major risks, and both can change costs within weeks.

hurts.title: Debts in dollars
hurts.text: Its leased planes create long dollar liabilities, so a weaker rupee causes exchange losses that can turn a profit into a loss.

hurts.title: Dependence on people and rules
hurts.text: Pilots, engineers and cabin crew are scarce, and changes to duty rules or labour unrest can force flights to be cancelled.

hurts.title: Geopolitics
hurts.text: Wars and airspace closures can force long detours and cut demand on international routes, the area where it is trying to grow.
